newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam to restrict access to satellite TV.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam to restrict access to satellite TV.

text.p: Vietnam plans to ban public access to television programmes beamed into the communist country by satellite and establish a limited redistribution service, according to new rules seen by Reuters on Tuesday.
A prime ministerial decision issued recently said that from January 1, only senior officials, government bodies, foreign agencies and diplomats can own receiving dishes for free access.

Foreign organisations, individuals and some Vietnamese nationals or businesses will be eligible to receive satellite programmes via a cable-based redistribution network run by state broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV).

A VTV official said Vietnamese customers would be charged 2,000,000 dong ($180) for connection and a monthly fee of 70,000 dong ($6.30). He said the company was negotiating with a number of foreign providers including the Discovery Channel.
Per capita income in Vietnam is around $220 per year.
Reasons for the decision were not immediately available, but the move appeared to be in line with ongoing efforts to tighten control over the flow of news and information.

The Government Office in Hanoi held a news briefing on Sunday for domestic journalists at which it warned that newspapers must bear full responsibility for their content and avoid disclosing Party and State secrets.
A month earlier, a resident U.S. journalist was refused a visa renewal -- effectively expelled. No official reason was given.
Hanoi regularly criticises foreign radio broadcasts, but has made little comment so far about television programmes being beamed into Vietnam from outside.
Satellite television is currently available in Vietnam, but the costs of receiving equipment have effectively prevented widespread access.
VTV has operated an informal redistribution service providing access to Cable News Network and STAR TV channels, but the official said this would now be halted.
He said VTV's new service would be encoded to comply with the rules and added that the company was hoping to distribute this more widely to viewers in Vietnam at a later stage.
